title: Thermodynamic Electric Toroidal Dipole and Intrinsic Longitudinal Spin Transport
authors: Taisei Yamanaka, Takumi Sato, Satoru Hayami
abstract: Electric toroidal dipoles (ETDs) characterize ferroaxial order, yet their bulk definition in periodic crystals has remained elusive because conventional multipole operators involve the ill-defined position operator. Here we formulate a thermodynamic ETD by coupling a spatially varying electric field to the relativistic spin-induced electric polarization. The resulting expression is gauge invariant and provides a bulk order parameter for ferroaxial phases. We further establish a direct relation between the chemical-potential derivative of the ETD and the intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity in insulating systems. To demonstrate the formulation, we construct a minimal ferroaxial extension of the Kane--Mele model. The ETD becomes finite exclusively in the ferroaxial phase and is strongly enhanced near a small band gap, accompanied by a sizable longitudinal spin current. Our results establish a thermodynamic theory of ETDs in crystalline solids and identify the longitudinal spin conductivity as a direct transport manifestation of ferroaxial order.
summary: This work develops a thermodynamic theory for the Electric Toroidal Dipole (ETD), a bulk order parameter characterizing ferroaxial electronic phases. By coupling the ETD to the spin-induced polarization, the authors establish a direct, quantitative relationship between the ETD and the intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity. This provides a new theoretical tool to diagnose and quantify ferroaxial order in crystalline solids.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of defining a gauge-invariant, bulk thermodynamic order parameter for the Electric Toroidal Dipole (ETD) in periodic crystals, and linking it to intrinsic longitudinal spin transport.
main_result: The ETD is shown to be a finite order parameter exclusively in ferroaxial phases, and its chemical-potential derivative is directly proportional to the intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity.
method: The authors formulate the ETD thermodynamically by coupling a spatially varying electric field to the relativistic spin-induced electric polarization, utilizing Green's function and Kubo formalism techniques.
model_or_system: The study uses a minimal ferroaxial extension of the Kane--Mele model, which incorporates symmetry-breaking hopping terms ($H_{FA}$) to realize ferroaxial order in a honeycomb lattice.
key_observables: Electric Toroidal Dipole (ETD, $G_k$), intrinsic longitudinal spin conductivity ($\sigma_{z}^{xx}$), and the longitudinal spin current.
important_parameters: The ferroaxial coupling strength ($\lambda_{FA}$), the chemical potential ($\mu$), and the band gap size (controlled by hopping parameters like $t'$).
main_assumptions: The conventional definition of ETD fails in periodic crystals due to the ill-defined position operator, necessitating a thermodynamic formulation. The analysis also uses semiclassical Boltzmann theory in some contexts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the honeycomb structure and the effect of ferroaxial hopping on the band structure. Subsequent figures show the dependence of the ETD ($G_z$) and spin conductivity ($\sigma_{z}^{xx}$) on the chemical potential and the strength of the ferroaxial coupling.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the thermodynamic definition of the ETD. It then applies this framework to the Kane-Mele model, demonstrating that the ETD is non-zero only when ferroaxial symmetry is broken. Finally, it derives a quantitative relationship linking the ETD's derivative to the longitudinal spin conductivity.
why_interesting: While focused on topological/symmetry physics, the rigorous derivation of a bulk, gauge-invariant order parameter and its direct link to a measurable transport coefficient (spin conductivity) provides a powerful theoretical tool for characterizing novel electronic phases in condensed matter systems.
